_comment: Probes for the triggering eval, kept OUT of the script on purpose.
The version this was extracted from had its probes as a literal inside the script -- 483 of
740 lines, and every one of them naming an internal identifier. The mechanism was portable;
the data was not, and nothing separated them. So the data lives here now, and the script is
the part you can hand to somebody else unchanged.
THE NON-TRIGGERING PROBES ARE THE HARD HALF, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE LESSON OF THE FILE.
A skill almost never fires on the weather. It fires on its NEIGHBOUR -- the skill next to it
that describes adjacent work in the same vocabulary. Probing with easy negatives ('what is
the capital of France') reports an accuracy the skill has not earned, because it measures a
confusion nobody was going to make. Every non-triggering probe below is aimed at a sibling,
and the comment says which one. If you cannot name the neighbour a probe defends against,
Four and four is the convention, not a rule the script enforces: enough that one miss is
visible against a threshold, few enough that a full run stays affordable. Vary the phrasing
-- four rewordings of one sentence measure one thing four times.
'exempt' is an allow-list of skills deliberately not probed, each with the reason. Keep it
SMALL and specific. It is the one place a coverage gate can be silenced, so an entry without
a reason is a silencer rather than a decision -- the script rejects one.

triggering: The checkout alert just fired. Is this a sev1?
Latency is climbing and I don't know if I should page anyone.
Something is wrong in production right now -- help me work out how bad.
Triage this: error rate up, no deploy in the last day.
non_triggering: We resolved it an hour ago. Help me draft the postmortem.
Write down the steps for failing over the database next time.
Explain what a service level objective is.
Refactor this retry loop to use exponential backoff.
_neighbours: 1 -> incident-writeup: same incident, but it is over. Tense is the only tell.
2 -> runbook-author: same subject matter, but the audience is a future reader.
3, 4 -> ordinary work, to keep one easy negative in the set as a floor.

triggering: The incident is closed. Write up what happened.
Draft the post-incident review from this timeline.
What should the writeup say about the cause?
Turn these notes from yesterday's outage into a review document.
non_triggering: The alert is firing now -- how bad is this and who do I wake?
Document the failover procedure so the next person can follow it.
Summarise this design document for the team.
_neighbours: 2 -> runbook-author: 'document' is the shared trigger word, and the likeliest collision.
3 -> a generic summarisation request, which any writing skill will over-claim.

triggering: Write a runbook for rotating the signing keys.
Turn this procedure into something the on-call can follow at 3am.
Update the runbook -- the second step doesn't work any more.
What steps and checks should the deploy procedure have?
non_triggering: Write up the outage we had on Tuesday.
The pager just went off. What is the next action?
Review this pull request for correctness.
Explain how our deploy pipeline works.
_neighbours: 1 -> incident-writeup: both produce a document about an operational event.
4 -> explanation, not procedure. The nearest thing to a false positive in normal use.
